key_figures.quote: Originally there was one licensing regime for commercial production of salmon and trout, while today there are ten different systems.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norwegian commercial salmon and trout aquaculture has shifted from one licensing regime to ten different systems.

key_figures.quote: At the same time, there has been a strong concentration of companies, where ten companies are currently responsible for about 70% of total production [44].
key_figures.statement: The author reports that ten companies were responsible for about 70% of Norwegian aquaculture production at the time of writing, citing [44].

key_figures.quote: Municipalities and county municipalities that previously did not receive any compensation for the use of local coastal areas, have now received an annual production fee as well as 40% of the payments for new capacity to the Aquaculture Fund.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norwegian municipalities and county municipalities receive an annual production fee and 40% of payments for new capacity to the Aquaculture Fund.

key_figures.quote: When the first temporary fish farming act was passed in 1973, there were 287 fish farms of very different sizes.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norway had 287 fish farms of different sizes when the first temporary fish farming act was passed in 1973.

key_figures.quote: From 1985–2002, there were no ordinary allocation of new licenses.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norway had no ordinary allocations of new aquaculture licenses from 1985–2002.

key_figures.quote: The coast was divided into 13 production areas, where the number of lice affecting wild salmon and trout would be decisive for further growth.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norway's coast was divided into 13 production areas under the traffic light system, with lice effects on wild salmon and trout determining growth.

key_figures.quote: In green areas, growth can be 6% every other year. In yellow areas, production should be kept stable, while production in red areas must be reduced by 6%.
key_figures.statement: The author describes the traffic light system's Norwegian production rules: growth of 6% every other year in green areas, stable production in yellow areas, and a 6% reduction in red areas.

key_figures.quote: As can be seen, the special licenses make up 21% of the total number of licenses, and 17% of the total MAB capacity.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that special-purpose licenses made up 21% of all licenses and 17% of total maximum allowable biomass capacity in Norway.

key_figures.quote: When the application period expired in November 2017, the Directorate of Fisheries had received 104 applications requesting 892 standard licenses (780 tons MAB).
key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norway's development-license application period, ending in November 2017, yielded 104 applications requesting 892 standard licenses (780 tons MAB).

key_figures.quote: By the end of 2020, 20 companies had received development licenses for a total capacity of 80,000 tons of MAB, while two applicants are awaiting a final answer.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that by the end of 2020, 20 Norwegian companies had received development licenses for 80,000 tons of MAB, with two applicants awaiting a final answer.

key_figures.quote: Of 104 applications, 82 were rejected, and 70 of these applicants have appealed the rejection.
key_figures.statement: The author reports that 82 of the 104 Norwegian development-license applications were rejected, and 70 rejected applicants appealed.

key_figures.quote: According to ilaks [28] there are currently 31 land-based projects being planned in Norway, either based on RAS-technology or flow-through systems.
key_figures.statement: The author cites ilaks [28] for 31 land-based aquaculture projects being planned in Norway at the time of writing.

pq_notes.A0: The author’s review presents licensing as a central instrument determining whether production can occur and where. A production license sets a volume in maximum allowable biomass, while a separate site license permits farming in a particular area; both are required. The article describes a shift from allocation based on discretionary social, regional and industry goals toward growth regulation through the traffic light system. That system uses lice effects on wild salmon and trout in 13 production areas to set growth or reduction. Site access also depends on other state agencies with veto powers under their sector laws, and municipalities must make space available through coastal zone planning in some allocation rounds. The article notes that coastal competition has become more acute and social acceptance remains a problem.
pq_notes.A1: The author’s account identifies access to a suitable site and the licensing regime as interacting constraints: a production license does not itself authorize operation at a site, and both production and locality licenses are required. Site availability is shaped by municipal coastal zone plans, sector-agency veto powers, and competing interests. Production opportunities also depend on the license category: ordinary commercial licenses are subject to traffic-light growth rules, while special-purpose licenses follow different criteria and are generally not subject to the same restrictions. Land-based and post-smolt production can avoid or reduce some sea-based constraints, but entail investment and emissions requirements. The author also describes sea lice as the sole environmental indicator used in the traffic light system, while fish health and environmental concerns have influenced earlier allocation criteria.
pq_notes.A2: The author describes a two-stage arrangement for special-purpose licenses: a production license is granted, but the operator must also obtain a site license; in some cases the Directorate of Fisheries can require a specified site. For development licenses, applicants submit project plans and proposed measurement criteria and milestones, which inform assessment and later conversion decisions. The review finds that evaluating these applications took much longer than expected, reflecting the scope and complexity of assessing innovation and investment. Of 104 development-license applications, 82 were rejected and 70 of the rejected applicants appealed; few appeals had been overturned by the Ministry at the time described. The segment does not give a general account of the ordinary site-application sequence or identify the most common site-stage delays.
pq_notes.A4: The author argues that licensing reallocates access from market selection to public administration, so authorities become responsible for allocation outcomes and exercise political and managerial discretion. License allocation has shifted from free permits toward auctions and, to a lesser degree, fixed prices; ordinary commercial licenses were reported in the abstract as trading at USD 15–20 million for a standard license of 780 tons MAB. Special-purpose licenses are granted free of charge but may offer a route to cheaper commercial capacity, an unintended consequence the author says has been underestimated. Development licenses can be converted to commercial licenses for a fixed price of NOK 10 million. Municipalities and county municipalities receive an annual production fee and 40% of payments for new capacity to the Aquaculture Fund. The segment discusses these arrangements but does not provide a full assessment of how costs and benefits are distributed among all stakeholders.
pq_notes.A5: The author’s review draws on document analysis, published studies, public reports, inspections, award and rejection letters, consultation responses, and interviews with officials, politicians and industry participants. For the traffic light system, the Institute of Marine Research acted as the government’s most important adviser, and growth decisions rely on models of lice dispersion. Farmers were skeptical of the scientific basis, while the author notes that the system uses only salmon lice as its environmental indicator; environmental critics sought additional indicators such as mortality, escapes, local pollution and use of medical substances. New technologies—including land-based systems, RAS, closed or semi-closed cages, post-smolt production and offshore systems—may change production and siting options. The author also notes uncertainty about whether planned land-based projects can secure financing and meet technical and emissions requirements.
pq_notes.A6: The author identifies increasingly acute competition for coastal space and significant social-acceptance problems for the industry. Aquaculture must be reconciled with the objectives enforced by state agencies that can veto access to a locality under sector laws; offshore development will also need coordination with fisheries, petroleum activities and offshore wind. In the 2003 allocation round, permits were restricted to municipalities able to present a coastal zone plan making space available for aquaculture. Conflicts also arise within the licensing system: farmers in production area 4 challenged reductions in maximum allowable biomass as unfair collective punishment, but lost in court. The author treats this protest, alongside criticism from environmentalists and farmers, as evidence that the traffic light system is not accepted as legitimate by all parties. The review does not set out a general model of legitimate decision-making.
pq_notes.A7: The segment does not present a dedicated set of measures that the industry itself should apply to make spatial use sustainable. The author does describe industry-driven and industry-requested initiatives that may affect efficiency: development licenses were intended to support significant technological innovation and investment, while larger post-smolt production can reduce time spent at sea and use sea-based MAB capacity more efficiently. Green licenses required new production methods intended to reduce sea lice and escapes, but the author says that experiment only to a limited extent created new technological solutions that also reduced environmental impact and addressed the area challenge. These are descriptions of licensing schemes and technologies, not a direct prescription for industry-led spatial management.
pq_notes.A8: The author’s account makes salmon lice a central production and regulatory concern: the traffic light system uses modeled lice effects on wild salmon and trout to determine growth in production areas. Farmers were skeptical of the scientific basis, which relied mainly on lice-dispersion models. Green licenses were designed to reward methods intended to reduce lice problems and escapes. The review also notes that larger post-smolt production reduces the time fish spend at sea and hence reduces salmon-lice problems. Special-purpose salmon may be co-located with ordinary production and subject to the same inspections, including lice counting and internal-control routines. The segment does not explain water connectivity between farms or provide a broader analysis of biosecurity and disease transmission.

key_figures.statement: The author reports that a standard Norwegian production license is valued at NOK 150–200 million and carries 780 tons of MAB.

key_figures.statement: The author reports that Norway’s license system had operated for almost 50 years under changing political regimes.

pq_notes.A0: The author describes a dual system: production growth is controlled through the traffic-light system, while municipalities determine where aquaculture may operate through plans under the Planning and Building Act. The central government asks counties and municipalities to allocate sufficient area for desired industry growth while also considering environmental and other societal interests. In practice, decisions involve multiple authorities and overlapping responsibilities, with trade-offs among growth, protection, food safety, animal welfare, environmental concerns and ownership. The author argues that the resulting administrative structure is cumbersome and internally conflicted. Coastal competition is intense, and aquaculture has no special priority among the users seeking space.
pq_notes.A1: The author identifies site availability, production capacity and regulation as interacting constraints. Companies can relinquish less favorable sites in exchange for more MAB at better sites, while access to new sites can be contested by multiple firms and prioritized by county aquaculture managers using a discretionary assessment of need. Site carrying capacity depends on water-body condition, organic loading, sediment chemistry, chemical use, benthic composition, currents, water exchange and biomass; the author says there is no direct conversion from bottom-survey results to MAB. The traffic-light system regulates production growth using salmon lice as its current indicator, but its application and special-purpose licenses can complicate environmental controls. Fish health appears through examples of high mortality and salmon lice, but the segment does not discuss disease transmission between farms.
pq_notes.A2: The segment does not provide a full step-by-step account of an ordinary site application. It says site allocation occurs under the Planning and Building Act, with municipalities deciding in principle where aquaculture may be practiced, and several authorities involved in establishment and operation. The author identifies laborious evaluation of new applications and processing of appeals as administrative burdens, alongside complex overlapping responsibilities. Where companies seek the same or nearby sites, county aquaculture managers prioritize applicants based on who has the “greatest need”; the author notes substantial discretion and cites legal criticism that conflicts over access should be regulated by law or regulations. Development-license applications were evaluated by the Directorate of Fisheries, with judgments about investment and innovation subject to administrative and political discretion.
pq_notes.A3: The author says environmental carrying capacity is determined site by site through assessment of natural treatment capacity, organic loading from aquaculture and other sources, sediment chemistry, chemical agents, benthic composition, current conditions, water exchange, fjord thresholds, and site biomass and production. The result is expressed as MAB, but the author stresses that there is no direct correlation between a bottom survey and MAB, nor a simple calculation from environmental condition to allowable biomass. Effects at a given MAB can differ between localities. This creates professional discretion and makes site comparisons difficult. The traffic-light system uses salmon lice as an objective indicator for production-area decisions, but thresholds and recommendations remain subject to administrative and political judgment; the segment does not describe a formal cumulative-effects assessment method.
pq_notes.A4: The author explains that the high value of production licenses supports companies’ balance sheets and creditworthiness, while selling new capacity provides revenue to the state and municipalities. Special-purpose licenses can provide a cheaper route to increased production than ordinary capacity, and the author says they had grown to over 17% of total MAB capacity. Development licenses are characterized as a substantial risk reduction or subsidy, with cited research finding that the scheme primarily benefited larger companies and prioritized technological solutions. Site allocation also distributes local economic benefits: municipalities may want to favor locally owned firms for their multiplier effects, but currently lack that opportunity. The author reports that collaboration on siting could yield gains if winners can compensate losers, and notes that farmers prioritize voluntary cooperation partly to avoid mandatory arrangements.
pq_notes.A5: The author describes decisions as relying on environmental surveys and expertise concerning water quality, sediment, benthic communities, currents, water exchange and biomass, as well as salmon-louse counts used in the traffic-light system. However, site carrying capacity cannot be calculated directly from bottom-survey results, and environmental effects at equal MAB may differ by site. The author also notes that salmon-louse counting itself involves discretion until mechanized. Recommendations from the Institute of Marine Research are subject to political review, and development-license judgments about technological innovation also involve administrative discretion. The segment argues that the system’s claimed objectivity is therefore incomplete. It proposes neutral third-party certification for closed or semi-closed technology as a possible way to verify zero lice emissions.
pq_notes.A6: The author describes intense competition for coastal space among aquaculture and other sea-area users, with more stakeholders seeking influence and several interests having veto opportunities. Conflicts also arise when firms compete for the same site, when municipalities wish to favor locally owned companies, and when environmental and industry interests disagree about traffic-light thresholds. The author says decisions in these settings retain substantial administrative and political discretion, which can expose them to lobbying. Legitimacy is central and applies to all sea-area users, not only salmon farmers; the traffic-light system remains controversial, while weak oversight and exceptions for special-purpose licenses undermine the logic and legitimacy of regulation. The author points to inter-municipal cooperation and possible compensation of losers as routes toward more effective area planning.
pq_notes.A7: The author reports that fish farmers prioritize voluntary cooperation on localization, in part because failure to cooperate could lead to mandatory joint de-licensing, fallowing or synchronized smolt release. Cooperation among farmers in the same area is also identified as a possible way to use space more effectively, with gains dependent on mechanisms for compensating those who lose. The segment discusses technological development, including closed or semi-closed systems intended to reduce lice, escapes and discharges, and proposes certification followed by an auction for capacity as one possible policy design. It also notes that firms can concentrate production on better sites by giving up less favorable locations. These are proposed or discussed measures, not evidence that all have been adopted.
pq_notes.A8: The segment addresses salmon lice as the traffic-light system’s current environmental indicator and says lice emissions would need to be zero under a proposed scheme for certified closed or semi-closed technology. It also identifies escapes and discharges as problems that new technologies might reduce. High mortality following an algae invasion in Nordland and Troms in 2019 is cited as an occasion when MAB regulation was adjusted. However, the segment does not explain biosecurity arrangements, water connectivity between farms, or how connectivity affects disease transmission and farm operations.
